1. Sleep duration (insufficient or excessive)

If sleep patterns show insufficient sleep, then extending the sleep period is recommended.

If sleep patterns show excessive time in bed (usually not always filled with sleep), then limiting time
in bed is recommended.

In both cases, increasing or decreasing the sleep period slowly is the most effective way to facilitate
patient compliance and not accidentally introduce sleep quality issues.

If sleep patterns are variable (more than an hour difference between weekday to weekend, or 30
minutes or more difference in daily bedtimes and waketimes), stabilize the sleep schedule by
establishing a consistent waketime and work backwards to identify the appropriate bedtime for the
patient's sleep need.

As with extending or shortening the sleep period, stabilizing requires slow change to promote

adherence and feasibility.

1. Consider what is causing instability in the sleep schedule. Is it due to just a difference in timing
(.e., bedtime and waketime on weekdays are earlier or later than on weekends), sleep duration
differing on weekdays compared to weekends (i.e., sleep duration on weekdays is shorter or
longer than the sleep duration on weekends), or a combination of both (e.g., weekday bedtime
and waketime are not only earlier or later than on weekends but sleep duration also differs
between weekdays and weekends)?

2. If the issue is solely timing, then start minimizing this difference by 15-30 minutes per week.
This usually means shifting the weekend bedtime and waketime earlier, as most people delay
their schedules on the weekends.

a. For example, a patient has a schedule that shows a weekday bedtime of 10:00 pm and
waketime of 6:30 am, while on weekends bedtime is 1:00 am and waketime is 9:30 am.
Start week one by shifting the weekend schedule so that bedtime is 12:45-12:30 am and
waketime is 9:15-9:00 am.

(e.g., patient goes to bed at 11:00 pm nightly but wakes at 6:00 am on weekdays and 10:00
am on weekends), then the goal is to match the bedtime and waketime on both weekdays and
weekends. Using this example, weeknight sleep duration is insufficient (7 hours) while weekend
sleep duration is excessive (11 hours). The goal would be to bring this to a central point of actual
need (average the sleep duration across the 7-day week).

GLOSSARY

Actigraph: an accelerometer with algorithms specifically for estimating sleep.

Adenosine: a ribonucleoside comprised of adenine bound to ribose, with vasodilatory, antiarrhythmic, and
analgesic activities. Accumulates in the brain throughout wakefulness to trigger sleep onset.

Advanced circadian phase shift (advanced phase shift): occurs when the master circadian clock shifts
earlier than the “normal” social clock, resulting in biological processes and behaviors that occur earlier and
out of syne with “normal.”

Ambient temperature: temperature of the surrounding environment.

Blue light: a specific range within the spectrum of light. Blue light creates greater melatonin suppression at
lower intensities and shorter durations and has disruptive nighttime effects.

Central oscillators: found in the suprachiasmic nucleus (SCN, see below), which is the main internal
“clock” and pacemaker.

Circadian rhythm: a biological process that regulates physiologic functions and behaviors over a 24-hour
period that aligns with the light-dark cycles. It's also known as the “master clock.” The circadian rhythm is
regulated by endogenous oscillators.

Delayed circadian phase shift (delayed phase shift): occurs when the master circadian clock shifts later
than the “normal” social clock, resulting in biological processes and behaviors that occur later and out of
sync with “normal.”

Endogenous or internal circadian oscillators: the molecules, cells, and tissues that make up the body’s
“internal clock.” They produce oscillating (alternating) currents through self-regulating positive and negative
feedback loops that produce the circadian rhythm. Endogenous oscillators include both the central and
peripheral oscillators.

Entrainment: the ability to be brought into a rhythm.

Inputs: the external and environmental factors that can entrain the circadian rhythm, often via interaction
with modifiers and operators. Modifiers are things that change the amount of “input” that gets to the body's
operators. Operators are the body's reaction or response to the modified inputs.

Melatonin: a natural hormone that is made in the pineal gland that helps regulate sleep and wake cycles.

Non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM): comprised of sleep stages 1 through 3; one of two types of
sleep and, after infancy, the first one we enter when falling asleep.

Outputs: the behavioral and physiological consequences of the operators.

Peripheral oscillators: these are present in many major organs in the body (kidneys, liver, heart, adrenal
glands, and pancreas). They allow for synchrony and alignment between the central and peripheral clocks.

Phase response curve: the response from the master circadian “clock” to light at different times during the
subjective day and night.

Polysomnography (PSG): also called a sleep study, this is an objective assessment using several
physiological measures to capture sleep and behaviors during sleep.

Rapid eye movement sleep (REM): one of two types of sleep and the second type we enter when
sleeping. Dreams occur most often during this stage.

Retinal ganglion cells (RGC): non-visual, light-sensitive retinal neurons that relay light intensity/spectra to
the suprachiasmic nucleus.

Suprachiasmic nucleus (SCN): the main body “clock,” or central “clock.” This is a portion of the
hypothalamus that regulates melatonin secretion and creates the circadian rhythm.
